clue.text: Standstill of workers after this reply to wage claim?

definitions.text: Standstill of workers after this reply to wage claim?

parts.words: Standstill of workers after this reply to wage claim?
parts.note: the phrase is both a curt refusal of a pay demand and a description of the strike that follows, when no work at all gets done

explanation.surface: A union's pay demand is flatly refused and the workforce downs tools.
explanation.walkthrough: The same two words do both jobs: said by the bosses they mean 'certainly not', and they then describe the idle factory floor.
explanation.definitionFit: The expression is an idiomatic flat refusal, and read literally it describes total inactivity.

clue.text: But no mod way-out gaol

parts.note: mod, short for modern, means new
a gate is a way out of an enclosure

explanation.surface: A prison that is not at all fashionable or avant-garde.
explanation.walkthrough: 'But no' warns that the name is ironic: Newgate was London's ancient and notorious prison, not new at all. 'mod' and 'way-out' look like 1960s slang for trendy.
explanation.definitionFit: Newgate was a notorious historic prison in the City of London.

clue.text: Heads on the floor'? What's up ?

definitions.text: Heads on the floor'? What's up ?

parts.words: Heads on the floor'? What's up ?
parts.note: a tossed coin landing face down: if one side is against the floor, the other side shows upward

explanation.surface: Someone sees heads lying on the ground and asks what is happening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What's up?' seems to mean 'what's going on?', but literally asks which face of a coin points upward.
explanation.definitionFit: The reverse of a coin is the side opposite the head.

clue.text: Not like Pussy's Owl to entangle one in knots

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: the letters of entangle are tied in knots, so rearranged

explanation.surface: A tangled mess is unlike the graceful owl of the nursery poem.
explanation.walkthrough: In Edward Lear's 'The Owl and the Pussy-cat', Pussy calls the Owl 'You elegant fowl!', so something unlike him lacks grace.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pussy-cat praises the Owl as elegant, so not resembling him means graceless.

clue.text: Hold hard, Raven.!

definitions.meaning: to hold something hard is to clutch it tightly
Barnaby Rudge's pet raven in Dickens's novel bears this name

explanation.surface: A command to a raven to hang on tight.
explanation.walkthrough: Dickens's Barnaby Rudge has a talking raven of this name, said to be modelled on Dickens's own pet.
explanation.definitionFit: Clutching firmly is one sense; the other is the name of a famous fictional bird.

clue.text: Get your plimsolls wet, 'might one say ?

definitions.text: Get your plimsolls wet, 'might one say

parts.words: Get your plimsolls wet, 'might one say
parts.note: plimsolls look like canvas shoes, but the Plimsoll line on a ship's hull goes under water when the ship carries too much

explanation.surface: Someone splashes through puddles in their gym shoes.
explanation.walkthrough: The Plimsoll line marks the safe loading depth on a ship's side; if it is submerged the ship has been loaded beyond the limit.
explanation.definitionFit: Loading a vessel beyond capacity sinks its load line below the water.

clue.text: Celebrated reply to, unlucky Edward's proposal

parts.note: no is the answer an unlucky suitor gets
Ted is a short form of Edward

explanation.surface: A famous refusal of a man's marriage proposal.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the clue as 'No, Ted' said in reply to Edward's proposal.
explanation.definitionFit: Noted means famous, well known.

clue.text: 61 surfeiting, The may sicken and so die" (T Night)

definitions.text: 61 surfeiting, The may sicken and so die" (T Night)

parts.words: 61 surfeiting, The may sicken and so die" (T Night)
parts.note: the missing word in Orsino's opening speech from Shakespeare's Twelfth Night

explanation.surface: A quotation from Shakespeare with a word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: Orsino's opening lines of Twelfth Night: 'Give me excess of it, that, surfeiting, The appetite may sicken, and so die.'
explanation.definitionFit: The word completes the quotation, meaning desire or hunger, here for music.

clue.text: Author names his own country

parts.note: a French writer whose pen name is the name of his homeland

explanation.surface: A writer gives the name of his native land.
explanation.walkthrough: Anatole France was the pen name of the French novelist Jacques Anatole Thibault.
explanation.definitionFit: This is both a nation and the surname of the Nobel-winning novelist Anatole.

clue.text: Not that it flows with milk in Africa

definitions.text: Not that it flows with milk in Africa

parts.words: Not that it flows with milk in Africa
parts.note: the river's colour word suggests milk, but the clue says it does not literally carry milk; it is an African river

explanation.surface: A denial that some African river is a land of milk and honey.
explanation.walkthrough: The White Nile is the branch of the Nile rising in East Africa; its name sounds milky, which the clue teasingly denies.
explanation.definitionFit: The name of this African river pairs the colour of milk with the great river of Egypt.

clue.text: Toby goes half Latin and gets drunk

indicators.note: only half of the name Toby survives, so its first two letters are taken

parts.note: per is a Latin word, meaning through or by

explanation.surface: Someone called Toby, partly speaking Latin, ends up inebriated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drunk' reads as an adjective but is the noun, a habitual drinker; a Toby jug is also a beer mug, which colours the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A toper is a heavy habitual drinker, a sot.

clue.text: A lemon ?Write it in

parts.note: the solution to a crossword clue is what you write into the grid

explanation.surface: Someone is handed a sour fruit and told to record it.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue talks about itself: what you write in the grid for any clue is this word.
explanation.definitionFit: A reply or solution is what a solver writes into the squares.

clue.text: Broken leg, bound to be caused by a heavy stick

indicators.note: the letters of leg and bound are broken up and reassembled

explanation.surface: A fractured leg is the sure result of a blow from a cudgel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broken' reads naturally as describing the leg in the surface, but it is the anagram signal for the two words that follow.
explanation.definitionFit: A bludgeon is a short club with a weighted end.

clue.text: Snare ' by trepan perhaps

indicators.note: the word trepan is only one possible arrangement of these six letters, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A trap is set by means of a trick.
explanation.walkthrough: Trepan is an old word for to lure or trap, so the fodder is itself a near-synonym of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To snare someone is to catch them in a trap.

clue.text: Swimmer upsets one young salmon in ten

indicators.note: the reversed pieces go inside the word ten
in a down clue, upsets turns the one and the young salmon upside down, reading them bottom to top

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
a parr is a young salmon

explanation.surface: A fish knocks over a single young salmon among ten.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'upsets' reverses the two pieces together, giving RRAPI, before they are placed inside the number.
explanation.definitionFit: A terrapin is a small freshwater turtle, which swims.

clue.text: Serving-men stand behind it

parts.note: serving-men suggests servants, but means tennis players serving, who stand behind the back line of the court

explanation.surface: Footmen and butlers wait in position behind something.
explanation.walkthrough: In tennis the server must stand behind the line at the back of the court.
explanation.definitionFit: The back line of a tennis court is where a server stands to start a point.

clue.text: From home, an away match

parts.note: sounds like football, but describes a couple running off from home to be married, a match made away

explanation.surface: A sports fixture played on the opponents' ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'match' means a marriage, not a game.
explanation.definitionFit: Running away secretly to marry is to leave home for a wedding.

clue.text: About fifty vie to 'be perfect

indicators.note: the word for vie goes about, around, the fifty

parts.note: to vie is to compete
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: Around fifty people strive for perfection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like 'approximately', but here it means around: COMPETE goes round L.
explanation.definitionFit: Complete means whole and perfect.

clue.text: Temporal extent of the French allotment

parts.note: du is French for 'of the'
a ration is an allotted share

explanation.surface: How long a French garden plot lasts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'allotment' suggests a vegetable plot, but here it means an allotted portion.
explanation.definitionFit: Duration is the length of time something lasts.

clue.text: The case for the receiver

parts.note: a grammatical case, the one marking the person who receives something, not a box for a telephone

explanation.surface: A box to hold a telephone handset.
explanation.walkthrough: In grammar the dative case marks the indirect object, the one given something.
explanation.definitionFit: The dative is the grammatical case of the indirect object, the recipient.

clue.text: Affected type, from the Paris model agency?

definitions.text: Affected type, from the Paris model agency?

parts.words: Affected type, from the Paris model agency?
parts.note: in French a word for a person who sits as a model is formed from pose plus the agent ending -eur, and in English it means a show-off

explanation.surface: A pretentious sort turns up from a French modelling firm.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'agency' is the French agent-noun ending: a person who poses, in Paris, is the same word English uses for an affected person.
explanation.definitionFit: A poseur affects attitudes or airs to impress others.

clue.text: So "Tripe !" made quaint repartee

indicators.note: the letters of so and tripe are made odd, rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone retorts 'Rubbish!' in an old-fashioned way of answering back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tripe' as a retort looks like the repartee, but SO and TRIPE are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A riposte is a quick sharp reply.

clue.text: A cross-section of the Church

parts.note: a representative sample of churchgoers, read instead as the section forming the crossbar of a cross-shaped church building

explanation.surface: A representative sample of churchgoers.
explanation.walkthrough: A cruciform church has arms crossing the nave; that cross part is the section meant.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the arm of a cross-shaped church running across the nave.

clue.text: Injunction from the Elsinore cellarage

parts.note: in Hamlet the Ghost, under the stage, repeatedly commands Hamlet's friends to take an oath

explanation.surface: A court order issued from a Danish castle's cellar.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet calls the Ghost 'this fellow in the cellarage' as it cries from below the stage.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ghost's repeated command orders the friends to vow secrecy.

clue.text: Chaps descend, to the hills of Somerset

parts.note: chaps are men
to dip is to go down

explanation.surface: Men go down towards the West Country hills.
explanation.walkthrough: The Mendip Hills are a limestone range in Somerset, a county in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Mendip is the name of a limestone range of hills in that English county.

clue.text: Sequel to Demonstration A, to end Private Lives

parts.note: demo is short for demonstration
B is the letter after A, its sequel

explanation.surface: A follow-up to a demonstration that ends a Noël Coward play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sequel to' A is B. Private Lives is a Noël Coward play; here it means the lives of army privates, which end when soldiers are released.
explanation.definitionFit: To discharge from the forces brings soldiers' service to an end.

clue.text: The ' bird, from King's Square, Mayfair

annotationWithheld.why: The ' bird, from King's Square, Mayfair (4): K for King and W1 for Mayfair fit, but no honest reading of 'Square' gives the I
annotationWithheld.clue: The ' bird, from King's Square, Mayfair

clue.text: Material one found in a rodent

indicators.note: the letter for one is located inside the rodent

parts.note: a vole is a small rodent
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A piece of fabric is discovered inside a small animal.
explanation.walkthrough: Voile is a thin semi-transparent fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: Voile is a light, sheer cotton or silk fabric.

clue.text: Skin's skin

parts.note: the outer layer of the skin itself, the skin belonging to the skin

explanation.surface: The covering of a covering.
explanation.definitionFit: The epidermis is the thin outermost layer of the skin, over the dermis.

clue.text: Notwithstanding, the only policy when opposed by this force ?

definitions.text: Notwithstanding, the only policy when opposed by this force ?

parts.words: Notwithstanding, the only policy when opposed by this force ?
parts.note: read 'notwithstanding' as 'not withstanding': a force that cannot be withstood leaves giving in as the only policy

explanation.surface: Advice on how to behave when faced with an overwhelming power.
explanation.walkthrough: Split 'Notwithstanding' into 'not withstanding': a force nobody can resist, as in the old puzzle of such a force meeting an immovable object.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that cannot be resisted or withstood is overwhelming.
